summary.text: For \(n=2,3,4\), padding any smaller candidate to respectively one, three, or nine digits and combining divisibility of it and its reversal forces the digit sum (via weighted digit-sum congruences modulo \(27\) or \(81\)) to be maximal, so every digit is \(9\). For \(n=t+5\), repeating the ten-digit block \(4899999987\) exactly \(3^t\) times gives a number and reversal divisible by \(3^{t+5}\): each repetition step multiplies both by \(1+10^{10\cdot3^t}+10^{20\cdot3^t}\), which contributes a factor of \(3\), while its \(10\cdot3^t\) digits make it strictly smaller than \(10^{27\cdot3^t}-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(m)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the ordinary decimal digits of \(m\). For a positive integer \(N\), call \(m\) admissible for \(N\) if
\[
m>0,\qquad N\mid m,\qquad N\mid \operatorname{rev}(m).
\]
Thus \(a(N)\) is the least admissible integer for \(N\), whenever an admissible integer exists. Equivalently, writing \(m=kN\), it is \(N\) times the least positive multiplier \(k\) for which \(N\mid\operatorname{rev}(kN)\).

We prove that, for every \(n\ge 2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

First we determine the three exceptional values exactly.

### A padding observation

It is useful to regard a decimal expansion in little-endian order. Thus if
\[
m=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i10^i,
\]
then its little-endian digit list is \((d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{r-1})\). If \(m<10^L\), append zeros to this list until it has exactly \(L\) entries. This does not change the represented number. Reversing this padded list may add zeros at the right-hand end of the usual decimal expansion of \(\operatorname{rev}(m)\). Consequently, the integer represented by the reversed padded list is
\[
10^{L-r}\operatorname{rev}(m).
\]
In particular, if \(N\mid\operatorname{rev}(m)\), then \(N\) also divides the integer represented by the reversed padded list. This lets us work with a fixed number of digits even when \(m\) has fewer digits.

### A three-digit lemma

Suppose \(d_0,d_1,d_2\in\{0,1,\ldots,9\}\), not all zero, and both
\[
A=d_0+10d_1+100d_2
\]
and its fixed-width reversal
\[
B=100d_0+10d_1+d_2
\]
are divisible by \(27\). Set
\[
S=d_0+d_1+d_2,\qquad T=d_1+2d_2.
\]
Since \(10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod {27}\) for \(i=0,1,2\),
\[
A\equiv S+9T\pmod {27}.
\]
Also, the coefficient of \(d_i\) in \(B\) is \(10^{2-i}\), and
\[
10^{2-i}\equiv 19-9i\pmod {27}
\]
for \(i=0,1,2\). Hence
\[
B\equiv 19S-9T\pmod {27}.
\]
As both \(A\) and \(B\) are divisible by \(27\), adding these two congruences gives
\[
27\mid 20S.
\]
Now
\[
23\cdot 20-17\cdot 27=1,
\]
so \(27\mid S\). The digits are not all zero, so \(S>0\), while each is at most \(9\), so \(S\le27\). Therefore \(S=27\), which forces
\[
d_0=d_1=d_2=9.
\]
Thus the only positive fixed-width three-digit string whose value and reversal are both divisible by \(27\) is \(999\).

We now apply this to admissible multiples of \(27\). The number
\[
999=37\cdot27
\]
is a palindrome, hence is admissible. Suppose there were a smaller admissible multiple \(m=k\cdot27<999\). Then \(0<m<10^3\). Pad its little-endian decimal digit list to length three. Its value remains \(m\), and its reversed padded value remains divisible by \(27\) by the padding observation. The three-digit lemma therefore says that \(m=999\), a contradiction. Hence
\[
a(27)=999.
\]

### A nine-digit lemma

Now suppose \(d_0,\ldots,d_8\in\{0,1,\ldots,9\}\), not all zero, and both the number
\[
A=\sum_{i=0}^8d_i10^i
\]
and its fixed-width reversal
\[
B=\sum_{i=0}^8d_i10^{8-i}
\]
are divisible by \(81\). Put
\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^8d_i,
\qquad
T=\sum_{i=0}^8 i d_i
=d_1+2d_2+\cdots+8d_8.
\]
For every relevant exponent, the binomial theorem gives
\[
10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod {81},
\]
because all terms from the quadratic term onward contain \(9^2=81\). Therefore
\[
A\equiv S+9T\pmod {81}.
\]
For the reversal, the coefficient of \(d_i\) is \(10^{8-i}\), so
\[
10^{8-i}\equiv1+9(8-i)=73-9i\pmod {81}.
\]
It follows that
\[
B\equiv73S-9T\pmod {81}.
\]
Adding the two divisibility relations yields
\[
81\mid74S.
\]
The explicit Bézout identity
\[
23\cdot74-21\cdot81=1
\]
then implies \(81\mid S\). Since the digits are not all zero, \(S>0\), and since there are nine digits each at most \(9\), \(S\le81\). Thus \(S=81\), forcing every digit to equal \(9\). Consequently, the only positive fixed-width nine-digit string whose value and reversal are both divisible by \(81\) is
\[
999999999.
\]

The number \(999999999\) is itself admissible for \(81\), since it is a palindrome and
\[
999999999=12345679\cdot81.
\]
If a smaller admissible multiple \(m=k\cdot81
e0\) existed, then \(m<10^9\). Pad its decimal expansion to nine digits. Both the padded value and the reversed padded value would be divisible by \(81\), so the nine-digit lemma would force \(m=999999999\), contradicting its strict inequality. Therefore
\[
a(81)=999999999.
\]

Finally,
\[
a(9)=9.
\]
Indeed, \(9\) is a palindrome and is divisible by \(9\), while every positive multiple of \(9\) is at least \(9\).

These three evaluations already give the desired equality for \(n=2,3,4\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
n=2:&\quad a(3^2)=a(9)=9=10^{3^0}-1,\\
n=3:&\quad a(3^3)=a(27)=999=10^{3^1}-1,\\
n=4:&\quad a(3^4)=a(81)=999999999=10^{3^2}-1.
\end{aligned}
\]

It remains to prove that equality fails for every \(n\ge5\). We do so by constructing a much shorter admissible multiple.

### The repeated-block construction

Let
\[
C=4899999987,
\qquad
C^{\mathrm R}=7899999984=\operatorname{rev}(C).
\]
For each \(t\ge0\), define \(W_t\) to be the decimal integer formed by concatenating \(3^t\) copies of the ten-digit block
\[
4899999987.
\]
Its reversal \(R_t=\operatorname{rev}(W_t)\) is therefore formed by concatenating \(3^t\) copies of
\[
7899999984.
\]
There are no issues with disappearing leading zeros, because both blocks begin and end with nonzero digits. Both \(W_t\) and \(R_t\) have exactly \(10\cdot3^t\) decimal digits.

We claim that
\[
3^{t+5}\mid W_t
\quad\text{and}\quad
3^{t+5}\mid R_t
\qquad(t\ge0).
\]
For \(t=0\), direct division gives
\[
4899999987=243\cdot20164609,
\qquad
7899999984=243\cdot32510288,
\]
and \(243=3^5\). This proves the base case.

For the induction step, let
\[
L=10\cdot3^t.
\]
Since \(3^{t+1}=3\cdot3^t\), the block string defining \(W_{t+1}\) consists of three consecutive copies of the entire string defining \(W_t\). Hence
\[
W_{t+1}=W_t\bigl(1+10^L+10^{2L}\bigr).
\]
The same reasoning applies to the reversed strings:
\[
R_{t+1}=R_t\bigl(1+10^L+10^{2L}\bigr).
\]
Because \(10\equiv1\pmod3\), one has \(10^L\equiv1\pmod3\), and consequently
\[
1+10^L+10^{2L}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Thus this common factor supplies one additional factor of \(3\). If \(3^{t+5}\) divides both \(W_t\) and \(R_t\), then \(3^{t+6}\) divides both \(W_{t+1}\) and \(R_{t+1}\). Induction proves the claim.

Since \(W_t>0\) and \(3^{t+5}\mid W_t\), write
\[
W_t=k_t3^{t+5}
\]
with \(k_t>0\). Moreover,
\[
3^{t+5}\mid R_t=\operatorname{rev}(W_t).
\]
Therefore \(W_t\) is admissible for \(3^{t+5}\). By the defining minimality of the sequence,
\[
a(3^{t+5})\le W_t.
\]

On the other hand, because \(W_t\) has \(10\cdot3^t\) decimal digits,
\[
W_t<10^{10\cdot3^t}.
\]
The exponent in the conjectured all-nines value for \(n=t+5\) is
\[
3^{(t+5)-2}=3^{t+3}=27\cdot3^t.
\]
Since \(3^t>0\),
\[
10\cdot3^t<27\cdot3^t=3^{t+3}.
\]
Hence
\[
W_t<10^{10\cdot3^t}<10^{3^{t+3}}.
\]
Both inequalities are strict integer inequalities, so in fact
\[
W_t<10^{3^{t+3}}-1.
\]
For example, the first strict inequality places \(W_t\) at most one below \(10^{10\cdot3^t}\), while the second places that power at most one below \(10^{3^{t+3}}\); thus \(W_t\le10^{3^{t+3}}-2\).

Combining this with the admissibility bound gives, for every \(t\ge0\),
\[
a(3^{t+5})\le W_t<10^{3^{t+3}}-1.
\]
Putting \(n=t+5\), this says that for every \(n\ge5\),
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
In particular, equality is impossible for all \(n\ge5\).

We now finish the equivalence. If \(n\ge2\) and
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1,
\]
then either \(n=2,3,4\), or else \(n\ge5\). The latter alternative has just been ruled out by the strict inequality, so \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\). Conversely, the exact evaluations of \(a(9)\), \(a(27)\), and \(a(81)\) prove the equality for \(n=2,3,4\), respectively. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\ a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1\iff n\in\{2,3,4\}\ }
\]
for every integer \(n\ge2\).
